canberra.title: Man rescued after entering lion enclosure at Canberra zoo
canberra.snippet: A man had to be rescued after he entered a lion enclosure at Canberra’s zoo. Fortunately, both the man and the animals were unharme...
canberra.content:
Police were called after a man entered an animal enclosure at the National Zoo & Aquarium over the weekend. Photo: James Coleman.

A man had to be rescued after he entered a lion enclosure at Canberra’s zoo. Fortunately, both the man and the animals were unharmed during the incident.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said officers went to the National Zoo & Aquarium around 1:30 pm on Sunday (27 September) after hearing that a man had entered an animal enclosure at the zoo.

While police did not state which enclosure he entered, Region understands it was a lion enclosure.

“The man was safely removed from the enclosure and was transported to hospital for assessment,” the police spokesperson said.

“Neither the man nor any animals were injured as a result of the incident.”

A zoo spokesperson thanked police for resolving the matter.

“The quick and efficient responses by both zoo staff and ACT Policing ensured a good outcome to the incident,” they said.

canberra.title: Deficit $6 billion lower than forecast, as RBA meets to hike interest rates
canberra.snippet: The Federal Government is congratulating itself on the Final Budget Outcome and an underlying deficit $6 billion lower than the $28.3 bil...
canberra.content:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher say good economic management has lowered the deficit. Photo: Jim Chalmers Facebook.

The Federal Government is congratulating itself on the Final Budget Outcome and an underlying deficit $6 billion lower than the $28.3 billion forecast in the May budget.

But while the nation braces for what is widely anticipated to be another hike to the official interest rate tomorrow (29 September), the Federal Opposition says government spending remains woefully out of control.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers has credited the improvement to the bottom line to a $1.4 billion decrease in payments and a $4.6 billion increase in receipts.

It was not driven by commodity prices but by more investor income.

“In fact, mining profits came in lower than what was anticipated,” Dr Chalmers said.

“It is overwhelmingly from higher super and investor income than what we anticipated in the Treasury’s forecasts in May … We made a lot of progress in the budget, and we’ve continued to make even more progress since then.

“This multi‑billion‑dollar improvement has been delivered despite months of more severe global volatility.

“Responsible economic management is a defining feature of this government, and you can see that here.

“The bottom line is better than what we inherited, better than what was forecast at the election, and it’s improved again since the budget.”

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said spending less across some government portfolios, as well as “a couple of national partnership payments”, has helped the bottom line.

“We are investing in those services that people really rely on. But in the last budget we’ve found savings, including in the NDIS, of over $35 billion,” she said.

“So, we are doing our bit. I take responsibility for that, making sure that we’re getting the budget in better shape, that we are finding savings where we can.

“But also … people expect their hospitals to be funded, their schools to be funded, their aged care system to be funded, NDIS to be funded, the Defence area of government funded, all of these areas.

“The pressure is increasing, not decreasing, in that. So, we have to take decisions about how we meet all those pressures and run the budget at the same time.

“The deficit’s coming in lower than what we forecast at budget, and again that’s because we’re so focused on making sure we do our bit to help with the inflation challenge.”

The Coalition, however, says higher taxes Australians have paid have been squandered due to Labor’s “reckless spending”, which is keeping inflation and interest rates higher for longer, and hurting all Australians.

Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said Labor had been handed a “massive windfall revenue” and still can’t get its spending under control.

“This is Labor’s fiscal record – more tax, more spending, more debt,” Senator Hume said.

“After all that revenue, Australians are still being left with deficits as far as the eye can see, and future generations will be left to pay that bill.

“Labor had an opportunity to use higher tax receipts to repair the budget. Instead, it has squandered that revenue on a spending spree that is growing at almost twice the rate of the economy, and he still has no plan to pay down Labour’s trillion-dollar debt.

“Jim Chalmers and Katy Gallagher have turned crisis-level spending into business as usual.”

Most economists agree the Reserve Bank of Australia will hike interest rates again on Tuesday, when its board concludes its sixth meeting this calendar year.

It would be the fourth rise this year, and if it is a standard 25-basis-point increase, the official cash rate would reach a 15-year high to sit at 4.6 per cent.

Dr Chalmers said he would not anticipate the RBA’s decision, but he acknowledged “that a lot of Australians will be apprehensive” about the central bank’s deliberations.

“Our job [Federal Government] is to manage the budget and the economy in the most responsible way that we can,” the Treasurer said.

But shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said Dr Chalmers “keeps fuelling” inflation and higher interest rates through government spending.

“This announcement is a desperate attempt to distract Australians from the prospect of three more interest rate rises thanks to Jim Chalmers’ addiction to spending and inflation – including tomorrow,” he said.

“That will push many families and small businesses over the edge.”

Speaking in Tasmania Monday afternoon, Anthony Albanese said his government had supported tax cuts, free TAFE, and multiple health initiatives to help lower the cost of living.

“All aimed at making a difference, because we know people are doing it tough,” the Prime Minister said.

canberra.title: Vikings gets tick for smaller Jerrabomberra club but transparency concerns persist
canberra.snippet: The Vikings Group has won approval for a scaled-back version of its Jerrabomberra club project, but how it got there has left a bad taste...
canberra.content:
The revised Vikings development for Jerrabomberra. Capacity has been cut to 800 patrons. Image: Benson McCormack.

The Vikings Group has won approval for a scaled-back version of its Jerrabomberra club project, but how it got there has left a bad taste in the mouth of the community association that fought the proposal.

Jerrabomberra Residents Association president Margot Sachse said the process had been incredibly frustrating, and the lack of transparency appalling.

“We’re disappointed, of course, because we believe that it was in the wrong location, but we accept that the court’s made that decision,” she said.

“We just need to make sure that the club’s compliant with the conditions.”

Last year the NSW Southern Regional Planning Panel knocked back the original $36 million proposal with 150 poker machines for the Poplars Precinct, noting unacceptable social impacts and that the net benefits of the club to the community did not outweigh the anticipated harm.

But Vikings appealed to the NSW Land and Environment Court. They took a smaller project, essentially just the first stage, into a conciliation process with the Queanbeyan and Palerang Regional Council.

The result was a deal acceptable to both parties and the LEC gave it its blessing last week, along with conditions, particularly to contain noise. The Commissioner said that she was not required to evaluate the merits of the matters originally in dispute.

The development application, as amended, is now for a two-storey registered club with an entry pavilion and ground-level restaurant, bar, gaming and function areas, with capacity reduced to 800 patrons.

Vikings expects fewer than 100 gaming machines.

Operating hours have also changed. The café and bistro will close at 10 pm; outdoor areas will close at 9 pm Sunday to Thursday and 10 pm Friday and Saturday; and function rooms will close at 12 am. The poker machine lounge and lounge/bar will open Monday to Sunday from 9 am to 2 am. Operations, including the service of alcohol, will cease at 1 am, and patrons may remain on the premises until 2 am.

The proposal includes car parking for at least 154 vehicles, a 3 metre-high acoustic barrier, and landscaping, including pedestrian paths.

Vikings Group CEO Anthony Hill said the Group was pleased to have reached agreement with QPRC on a revised plan for the Poplars Club in Jerrabomberra.

Mr Hill said the approved proposal was materially different from the original application.

“We thank the local Jerrabomberra residents who expressed their support through emails and social media and attended our community information sessions, and we now commence the process of delivering them with a quality community club, as we have already done with Campbell & George in Queanbeyan,” he said.

Mr Hill said there was a lot to work to do before a start date could be set for construction, but the build was expected to take 12 to 18 months.

Vikings CEO Anthony Hill: pleased an agreement could be reached. Photo: Vikings.

Ms Sachse said that once the matter moved into confidential Court conciliation between Vikings and QPRC, the community had very little visibility of the negotiations that ultimately resulted in the amended proposal.

“It was basically just the council, who were representing the Southern Regional Planning Panel, and the applicants, and everybody else was excluded,” she said.

“We don’t even know what the discussions were on how they came about it because all of the conciliation process is confidential.

“So we don’t think that this process has the transparency that we expect that these sorts of things should have for neighbours and nearby residents.”

The Association believed the decision also raised a broader issue about gambling regulation across the ACT-NSW border.

While the ACT Government had recently announced a major package of reforms to reduce gambling harm, an ACT-based club had now received approval for a new poker-machine venue immediately across the NSW border, where its gaming operations will be regulated under NSW rather than ACT laws.

“Gambling policy in the Canberra region does not stop at the ACT border,” Ms Sachse said.

“Canberra residents will be able to readily access this venue, while the local impacts associated with traffic, parking, patron movements, noise and late-night activity will be experienced by the Jerrabomberra community.

“At a time when the ACT is actively seeking to reduce reliance on poker machines and strengthen gambling-harm protections, we believe there needs to be a broader discussion about what happens when gaming activity moves just across the border into NSW.”

The Association intended to raise the issue with the NSW Government, including the Premier, Deputy Premier and local State Member.

Ms Sachse said the Association had never opposed a new club in the area, just the location and scale of the proposal.

Community response would be mixed, depending on how close people lived to the site.

Noise conditions included independent acoustic compliance testing that must be undertaken 12 months and 24 months after an Occupation Certificate is issued, during peak operating periods and without prior notice to Club management.

If testing identified a noise breach associated with operations after midnight, the Club must cease operating at midnight until corrective measures had been completed and certified.

Ms Sachse said rigorous monitoring and enforcement of these conditions would now be critical.

“The Court process may be finished, but for residents the real test will be what happens once the Club is operating,” Ms Sachse said.

“The noise limits, patron caps and operating-hour conditions will only protect residents if they are properly monitored and enforced.”

canberra.title: Life’s a beach for Canberra’s outdoor volleyball village
canberra.snippet: Take off your shoes, sport! Canberra’s closest “beach” – only 12 minutes’ drive from the CBD – offers sun-soaked outdoor action with gold...
canberra.content:
Who needs a coastline to play beach volleyball? Not Lyneham Beach Facility on Thurbon Road. Photos: Volleyball ACT.

Take off your shoes, sport! Canberra’s closest “beach” – only 12 minutes’ drive from the CBD – offers sun-soaked outdoor action with golden sands between your toes.

“You could go to the Murrumbidgee, but we’re the main beach in town,” says Ciaran O’Rourke, Volleyball ACT’s general manager.

Fresh air, late afternoon sun and a competition setting you can dial up or down as easily as the indoor treadmill you may currently be pounding amid the remnants of 9-5 sweat – welcome to Lyneham Beach Facility on Thurbon Road, home of beach volleyball in the national capital.

“It’s a nice, relaxed vibe on the courts,” Ciaran says. “It genuinely feels like you’re down the beach in summer. There’s no escaping it.

“There’s a food van. Grab yourself a drink, relax with your mates and enjoy the atmosphere at the beach courts underneath Telstra Tower.

“It’s a beautiful sunset on a good evening.”

Don’t forget the frenetic on-court action. The traditional indoor game is no slouch when it comes to movement and energy. Ratchet that up a notch for the beach game.

Think Test cricket versus T20 or Super Rugby compared to Rugby Sevens.

“Beach volleyball’s more of a party atmosphere, tournament-style play, typically a lot faster and more furious, and more action-packed,” Ciaran says.

“It can be really intense. But the matches are short.”

Volleyball ACT Facilities. Photo: Roy Meuronen Photography

Photos: Roy Meuronen Photography.

Photo: Roy Meuronen Photography

Photo: Roy Meuronen Photography

Canberra beach volleyballer Tom Attrill in action in the 2023 ACT Open. Photo: Roy Meuronen Photography.

The sport’s briefer format provides another drawcard for a world always in a hurry.

“Matches last under an hour in beach volleyball,” he says. “There’s only so long you can try and pick yourself up off the sand!

“You’re talking 45 minutes on average, depending on how the game goes.

“It’s short and sharp.”

Compare this to 18 holes of golf, an afternoon of club cricket, nine innings of baseball or 21 ends on the bowls rink.

Beach volleyball on Lyneham’s eight sand courts and four grass courts also offers a range of options, starting with the Beach League competition.

Season 2 of 2026 Beach League starts the week of Monday, 12 October and ends Thursday, 17 December. The first match each afternoon starts at 5:30 pm, the last at 9:30 pm.

Registrations for Monday men’s pairs, Tuesday women’s pairs, Wednesday mixed pairs, and Thursday mixed fours close Sunday, 4 October (end of day). Everyone is welcome. No age limit; players range from about 15 to over 50.

Is it suitable for first-time players?

“Absolutely,” Ciaran says. “The Beach League is your introduction to beach volleyball, where you can either find a player for pairs or get a group of mates and play mixed fours to take the pressure off.

“Start in the bottom division, get used to playing. You don’t have to move around as much in fours on the same-sized court. But after half an hour on the sand, you’ll still feel it.

“It’s not such a big workout that you’re absolutely exhausted and can’t get through to the end of the game, either.”

More serious players can take on the six-event Beach Series, including the Sport Your Pride multisport event at Southwell Park on 14 November and ACT Open on 27-28 February, 2027.

The series forms part of the Australian beach tour where players earn points towards national rankings. And the rewards are worthwhile.

Australia recently secured spots for one male and one female competitor at the 2028 LA Olympics through the Asian qualifiers.

A group of Canberra players, who train at the Lyneham facility under their own coaches, also qualified six pairs for an Oceania event in the Cook Islands in a couple of weeks.

Ciaran says the representative successes, reaching back to the 2000 Sydney Olympics, underline the sport’s potential in the ACT – on and off the courts.

“We have the facility; we have the interest of a couple of hundred people in our beach volleyball community.

“We want to grow that number and the facility into a well-known part of the Canberra sporting community.”

And what should you wear on the beach volleyball court? Before you ask, bikinis and budgie smugglers are no longer part of the mandatory dress code.

Wear what’s comfortable and a similar-coloured shirt or singlet to your teammate(s).

Most players take the court barefoot. But wear beach socks for hot-day games and always bring a water bottle.

To register, book a court, or for more information about corporate bookings, visit Volleyball ACT.

canberra.title: Accused mall attacker granted bail despite alleged ‘danger’ to children
canberra.snippet: The young man accused of attacking two boys inside a Canberra mall has been granted bail after spending over a month in custody, although...
canberra.content:
An 18-year-old man allegedly assaulted two children at Westfield Belconnen on 14 August 2026. Photo: Westfield Belconnen Facebook, Michelle Kroll, Albert McKnight.

The young man accused of attacking two boys inside a Canberra mall has been granted bail after spending over a month in custody, although he cannot leave his home unless he is escorted by two of his family members.

The two boys, aged two and four, were with their mother at Westfield Belconnen on 14 August 2026 when they were allegedly attacked by the 18-year-old male stranger.

One child was allegedly kicked, while the younger boy was reportedly left with a broken nose.

The 18-year-old, whose name has been suppressed, was refused bail several days later. He spent about a month in custody before beginning his second bail application, which has continued for about 10 days.

Over this time, the ACT Magistrates Court has heard of his extensive disabilities, including that he apparently has the intellectual capacity of a 10-year-old.

The court has also heard prior allegations that he had assaulted multiple children in public. He allegedly pretends to be a car running them over when he is assaulting them.

On Monday (28 September), the man’s lawyer, Gillian Bilton of Legal Aid, proposed he be released on several strict bail conditions, essentially house arrest.

She said his family had taken several steps to secure their home.

“It is my submission it will be very difficult for this young man to leave that house,” she said.

Prosecutor Taden Kelliher said it was a very difficult bail application.

“He is a danger, to put it bluntly, to anybody, particularly children, he may come across,” he alleged.

But he accepted the man couldn’t remain in custody forever and said his office, “rather reluctantly”, would not oppose his release.

Special Magistrate Sean Richter granted bail on conditions including that the man not leave home unless in the company of two of his family members, either both of his parents or one of them with his brother, and only leave if going to a medical appointment or court.

He is also not allowed within five metres of children.

When asked whether he understood this last condition, the man said, “I won’t go like this … bang”, while hitting one hand into the other.

The matter was adjourned to 27 October.

The man has been charged with two counts of assault. No pleas have been entered.

australia.title: Larissa Waters steps down as Greens leader due to ill health
australia.snippet: Ballot for new leader expected next week after Waters quits to manage pre-existing kidney disease that has ‘declined significantly’ Get o...
australia.content:
Greens leader Larissa Waters has announced she will step down due to ill health, with a party room meeting scheduled for next week to choose her successor.

Waters revealed on Monday night she has been managing a pre-existing kidney disease, but that her health had “declined significantly over the course of recent months”.

She said while her prognosis for recovery was positive, the pressure of the party’s leadership, including additional travel demands, was detracting from a focus on her health.

Waters replaced Adam Bandt as Greens leader after the 2025 election, in which Bandt lost his lower house seat in a shock result.

But some Greens members have expressed frustration with the party’s position under Waters, including its cut-through with voters as the major parties haemorrhage support to One Nation.

  • Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Waters said in a statement she would take a period of medical leave, before returning to parliament to represent Queensland in the Senate.

“It has been a tremendous honour to be leader of the Greens, fighting for people and the planet,” she said.

“I’m really sad that illness means my time as leader has been cut short, but our movement needs a leader in good health to lead us to success at the next election.

“Passing the torch on to the next leader of the party will put them in the best position to take the Greens to the next election, fighting for people, not the corporate interests that run Labor, Liberals and One Nation.

“Our fight is too important, and it needs more time and energy than I am able to give while I focus on my recovery.”

She thanked her colleagues and doctors for their support, citing successes including negotiations with Labor on environmental law reforms and tougher gun laws introduced after last year’s Bondi Beach terror attack.

“I will keep working for the people of Queensland, for women’s safety and for climate action when I am able to return to parliament.”

Deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi, and high profile senators Sarah Hanson-Young, David Shoebridge and Nick McKim could contest the leadership ballot.

Waters was first elected to the Senate in 2011 but was forced to resign in July 2017 after discovering she held duel Canadian citizenship during parliament’s eligibility crisis.

After renouncing her citizenship, she returned to the upper house in September 2018 to fill a vacancy.

Waters was a co-deputy leader to Bandt, and to former leader Richard Di Natale at various times between 2015 and 2022.

As the party’s spokesperson for women, Waters played a role in shaping the independent parliamentary workplace watchdog based on recommendations from Kate Jenkins’ report into the culture in Parliament House.

The Greens have been reduced to a single lower house MP – Ryan’s Elizabeth Watson-Brown – after the May election, with minor primary vote swings against Bandt and two Queensland incumbents, Max Chandler-Mather and Stephen Bates.

The party maintains the losses were due to a drop in votes for the Liberal party favouring Labor candidates, as well as a reduction in favourable preference flows.

australia.title: Plan for controversial $1.2bn datacentre in Sydney scrapped due to ‘emerging’ regulations
australia.snippet: Developer Goodman Group says changes in government rules are behind decision to pull plug on ‘Project Mars’ in Lane Cove Get our new poli...
australia.content:
Plans for a controversial $1.2bn datacentre in Lane Cove in Sydney’s north have been withdrawn, with the developer blaming “emerging” regulations from the state and federal governments for the decision to pull the plug.

The “Project Mars” plans were withdrawn from the NSW planning portal on Monday, with the developer, Goodman Group, posting on its site that the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale datacentres had “evolved significantly”.

“Having considered emerging federal and state policy, Goodman has concluded that it will not progress with the development application.”

In August, the NSW government announced its new “fast-track” framework for datacentre applications that promised to assess applications within 75 days if the plans meet set principles, including applying “world-class” standards for noise and air pollution, imposing no net cost to consumers and communities and funding additional water and energy supply.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

It followed the federal government’s rules in July aimed at addressing growing community concerns with datacentre location choices, and energy and water use requirements, with legislation expected to hit the federal parliament early next year.

The Lane Cove proposal had become one of the main sources of criticism of the datacentre growth in Australia.

The proposal had been criticised by local residents due to its proximity to local schools, event spaces and green space, as well as the growing concerns about clustering with a number of datacentres planned or in operation in Lane Cove. Guardian Australia first reported the community concerns in May.

Lane Cove Responsible planning spokesperson Sasha Titchkosky said she was “absolutely ecstatic” at the decision to withdraw the plans.

“I think we could have all saved everyone a lot of hassle and heartache if we actually had an appropriate regulatory regime and the government at state and federal had jumped on this when we started calling for better regulation.

“There was a real regulatory gap and that’s causing issues all around the country with inappropriate datacentres being put forward that really don’t give communities any benefits.”

Titchkosky thanked Goodman Group for listening to community concern and withdrawing the proposal.

A spokesperson for Goodman Group declined to comment further, but pointed to the opening statement made by the company’s general manager for development, Ben McGilp, at last week’s hearing of the Senate inquiry into datacentres.

McGilp said the company supports “clear, consistent and evidence-based regulation that provides confidence for communities, governments and industry”.

The peak body for the sector, Data Centres Australia, warned the committee in its submission to the inquiry that the risk for Australia is not over-building datacentres but “under-building”.

“Turning the investment away does not reduce global data centre energy or water use, it simply redirects it to jurisdictions with weaker protections than Australia’s, while Australia forgoes the economic value and the sovereign capability.”

australia.title: After a dead whale washed up at a Perth beach, some took selfies. Others held their nose from the stench
australia.snippet: Local authorities have closed the beach for several kilometres and multiple sharks have been spotted in the area Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
Multiple sharks have been spotted swimming near a large, smelly whale carcass that has washed ashore at a popular capital city beach, drawing hundreds of onlookers.

Surf lifesavers found the dead animal at Perth’s City beach at about 7.30am on Monday and raised the alarm.

Local authorities closed the beach for several kilometres in each direction of the carcass, which appeared to be about six metres long.

Multiple sharks have been spotted in the area, including a five-metre great white.

“It is possible the carcass will continue to act as an attractant that could lead to sharks coming in close to shore along this stretch of coast,” the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development warned.

“People should exercise additional caution.”

The alerts come 10 days after 63-year-old Greg O’Neill was killed in a shark attack while swimming close to shore at Perth’s Sorrento beach, about 12km north of City beach.

Hundreds of onlookers gathered on Monday to view the whale.

“It’s sad, they’re such a beautiful animal,” a local, David Jones, said. Several dead whales had washed up on the same stretch of coast in the previous decade, he said.

Many onlookers took selfies in front of the massive carcass, while others held their noses to protect themselves from the stench.

The silhouettes of sharks could be seen in the waves, swimming up and down the coast.

Town of Cambridge mayor, Gary Mack, said it was important members of the public took heed of the warnings.

“This is not a time for taking risks,” he said.

Mack said authorities were assessing the carcass and it was likely to be removed from the beach on Tuesday.

“It seems at this stage the plan will be to remove the carcass on the back of a truck and take it to a landfill site,” he said.

The other option is to tow it out to sea, but Mack said that may prove difficult.

“There’s a bit of surf down there, and it’s rocking back and forth and appears to be wedged on the sandbar,” he said.

australia.title: Anthropic will not appear at Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres amid fallout from OpenAI hack
australia.snippet: Company behind Claude chatbot expected to attend separate Australian government hearing on AI next week Get our new political email , fre...
australia.content:
The chief executive of Anthropic will turn down an invitation to appear at a Senate committee hearing on AI this week, in the wake of the revelation that OpenAI agents had breached Australian government websites.

However, the company will make an appearance before another committee early next week.

The chair of the Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres, Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, wrote to OpenAI and Anthropic last week asking for their US-based chief executives to appear before the committee on Thursday this week.

The invite came after the prime minister’s revelation that OpenAI’s agents had infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Neither company’s executives could be compelled to appear before the Senate committee, given they are based outside Australia, and it is understood that Anthropic – the company behind Claude – will not attend the hearing this week.

It is understood the company’s local team is not in Australia, and the invite was considered last-minute. An alternative date for the hearing has been sought.

Anthropic is, however, expected to attend a separate joint standing committee hearing on AI next week. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, will not attend, but it is understood representatives of its Australian and US operations will appear.

The company has made a submission to that committee in which Anthropic warned that governments had a critical role in reinforcing a responsible approach to AI by industry, while also arguing that frontier AI was not just an economic capability but also a “national security capability”.

“It matters which countries build the most capable models, and on whose terms they are deployed,” Anthropic said in the submission.

“The most capable AI models are built in the United States. Broadening that development out to trusted allies like Australia is critical and will support efforts to ensure that the capability of democracies outpace those of authoritarian states.”

OpenAI was approached for comment. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, who was in the United States last week when announcing the hack, said he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”.

The finance and government services minister, Katy Gallagher, flagged new mandatory reporting rules could be introduced for AI data breaches. After criticism of the government’s slow response to the incident, Services Australia has put in place new procedures to ensure real-time monitoring of information sent to the public-facing email address used by OpenAI to report the hacking.

But Gallagher rejected Coalition claims the government had politicised the Medicare breach, rejecting suggestions Labor had delayed a public announcement or overstated the significance of the rogue agent’s actions.

“It is the first time that we’re aware that an agent acting on its own, not with the authority of OpenAI, was able to get into one of our data systems, and I think we did the right thing,” she said.

Cabinet was briefed on the ongoing investigation on Monday, as the company continued to cooperate with Services Australia and the intelligence agency, the Australian Signals Directorate.

Gallagher said the investigation would take a matter of weeks to be completed but confirmed the statistical website accessed in the incident had been decommissioned and the data transferred to a new portal.

The taskforce would also review how OpenAI’s agent had interacted with the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s website.

An obscure German wiki site that was reportedly hijacked and used as a message board for the agents to communicate with each other included messages showing the agents tried and failed to access the AIHW website data over multiple days in June this year, as first reported by the ABC.

Part of $160m in new funding for cybersecurity improvements at Services Australia, announced in the May budget, will be used for the response to the OpenAI incident.

“The kind of cyber protections of a public-facing website, versus our systems of government significance are quite different, and they are under constant, constant attention from people who would like to get in,” Gallagher said.

“Those systems are the ones that the upgrade will be focused on.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said every cyber-attack was serious, but criticised Albanese for waiting to reveal the incident publicly.

world.title: At least 27 dead after two mass shootings in South Africa, police say
world.snippet: Seventeen people killed near Johannesburg in suspected ‘illegal goldmining turf war’, as 10 killed in separate incident at barbecue venue...
world.content:
Two separate mass shootings near South Africa’s two biggest cities killed at least 27 people, as the country grapples with one of the world’s highest murder rates amid investigations into corruption and criminality within the police.

The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.

In a separate statement, police said 10 people had been killed in a mass shooting at an entertainment venue selling grilled meat, known as shisanyama, in Lwandle, near Cape Town. Another 11 people were wounded in that shooting. Police said they were searching for multiple suspects, without giving an exact number.

The two attacks happened days after a mass shooting by three gunmen at a house party near the east-coast city of Durban killed 11 people, including a pregnant woman.

No arrests had been made in the two latest mass shootings, police said.

South Africa has struggled with high rates of violent crime for years, but the series of mass shootings this week were shocking even to a country used to some of the highest violent crime rates in the world.

“This ​cannot go on like this,” South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, told local TV news channels. “This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going ⁠to continue pulling out all stops.”

Police in the province of Gauteng said on Sunday morning they had launched a manhunt for the unidentified eight suspects in the Johannesburg tavern shooting, with no arrests yet made.

“It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside,” a police spokesperson, Capt Tintswalo Sibeko, said in a statement.

“The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles. Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident.”

While many local residents did not want to speak about the shooting, one said that illegal goldminers were active in the area. Gauteng province’s police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one of their lines of inquiry was that the shooting was part of a “turf war in terms of illegal mining”.

Illegal miners, known as zama zamas, which means “to take a chance” in Zulu, are usually part of powerful gangs, with multiple mass shooting incidents around Johannesburg blamed on them in recent years.

Mthombeni also said Saturday’s shooting could have been retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago.

Western Cape police said they had set up a team led by serious violent crime detectives to investigate the Cape Town shooting, in which the gunmen entered the shinsanyama venue at about 1.46am on Sunday and starting shooting at customers.

“Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities,” the statement said. “Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained … Detectives are hard at work in search of the perpetrators of the shooting incident, with no arrests effected yet. The identities of the deceased persons will be released once their next of kin are informed.”

A police official said that “business jealousy might have been the issue”, citing reports that people had been buying cheaper alcohol elsewhere and then bringing it to the venue to drink.

South Africans are already reeling after the discovery of numerous women’s bodies near Johannesburg’s airport since July, most of which were found in the last few weeks. The killings led to renewed anger about high rates of gender-based violence in the country, and have piled pressure on police and politicians to do more about it.

Alongside this, the Madlanga commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police in televised hearings for the past year.

South Africa had a murder rate of almost 40 per 100,000 people in 2024, according to the UN office on drugs and crime. That was the ninth-highest in the world that year, with only Caribbean countries higher.

In the 12 months to 30 June, more than 22,700 people were murdered in South Africa, according to police data.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
world.snippet: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer Cape Town’s c...
world.content:
Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

“It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.

In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.

Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.

Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

“No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
world.snippet: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government There are growing fears of a retu...
world.content:
There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.

Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.

A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”

The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.

In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.

Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.

The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.

On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.

In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.

AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
world.snippet: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market Nils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s ...
world.content:
A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.

The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.

Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.

Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.

“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”

Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”

Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.

Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.

Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.

Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.

The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.

Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

world.title: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
world.snippet: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality One of South Africa...
world.content:
One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.

Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.

Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.

South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.

Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”

Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.

The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.

Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.

Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.

“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”

When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.

Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.

Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.
